title: Linear Search
description: The most basic search there is: scan sequentially, compare each item, stop when you find it -- a predictable **O(n)**.

sections.title: Introduction to Sequential Traversal
sections.content:
**Linear Search** is the most basic way to find something: check each element in order until you find the target or run out of elements.

No sorting, no recursion, no extra data structures -- it works on any array or linked list, making no assumptions about order.

Simple as it is, mastering its control flow -- boundary checks, pointer logic -- is the foundation for everything from binary search onward.

sections.title: Why Linear Search Matters
sections.content:
Real systems constantly deal with unsorted data -- attendance lists, error logs, small contact lists.

When data has no order, there's **no safe way to skip elements** -- you have to check each one.

Sorting costs O(n log n). If you only need one search, paying that cost just to unlock a faster search isn't worth it -- a direct O(n) linear search wins.
bullets: Works on **unsorted arrays** with no preprocessing.
Ideal for **small datasets or one-time queries**.

sections.title: Core Idea of Linear Search
sections.content:
Compare each element to the target, in order, starting at index 0. Match found → return the index immediately. Reach the end with no match → return a not-found value (typically -1).

Unlike Binary Search, nothing gets eliminated -- elements are simply checked one by one. That guarantees finding the target if it exists, but worst case means checking everything.

sections.title: Searching Through an Array
sections.content:
Searching for 11 in [3, 8, 5, 11, 2]: compare 3, 8, 5 -- no match. Compare 11 -- match! Return index 3, no need to check the rest.

Searching for 10 (not present): every element gets checked, no match, return -1.

Worst case is always the same shape: target at the end, or missing entirely -- every element gets examined.

sections.title: Advanced Traversal Paradigms
sections.content:
A few variations on the basic scan:

**Reverse Traversal for Terminal Tracking:** need the *last* occurrence of a value? Scanning front-to-back means reading the whole array to be sure. Start at `len(arr) - 1` and count down instead -- the first match found is guaranteed to be the last occurrence, so you can exit immediately.

**Boundary Sanitization (Range Searching):** searching within a `start`/`end` sub-range needs those bounds clamped first -- negative start to 0, overflowing end to `len(arr) - 1` -- or you risk an Index Out of Bounds crash.

**Multi-Target Extraction:** need every index where a value appears? No early exit allowed -- scan the whole array, appending each match's index to a results list. That pushes space from O(1) up to O(n).

sections.title: Code Implementations and Execution Flow
sections.content: A search function needs to return correctly on both success and failure -- exit early on a match, fall back to a not-found value once the loop completes.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Worst case is **O(n) time** -- double the array, double the worst-case comparisons.

Space is **O(1)**: just a loop counter and a return value, no new arrays (unless doing Multi-Target Extraction).

At n=10 million, that's noticeable. At n=1 billion, it's impractical -- exactly when sorted data and binary search become worth it.

subsections.title: The Omega Bound (Ω): Best Case
subsections.content: **Ω(1)** -- the target is the very first element. Searching for 8 in [8, 3, 5, 1] takes one comparison.

subsections.title: The Big-O Bound (O): Worst Case
subsections.content: Target at the end or missing entirely. Searching for 10 in [3, 8, 5, 11, 2] checks every element before returning -1 -- n comparisons for n elements.

sections.title: Linear Search vs Binary Search
sections.content:
Linear Search: works on unsorted data, simple, but slow at scale. Binary Search: needs sorted data, but halves the search space every step.

At 1 million items: linear search up to 1,000,000 comparisons; binary search ~20 -- **50,000x faster**.

But binary search has a cost of entry: unsorted data needs an O(n log n) sort first. Linear search wins when the array is small, you're only searching once, or you're working with a linked list where random access is expensive.

subsections.title: Advantages
bullets: Great for **small datasets or one-off queries**.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: **Optimized searches** win once data is structured.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Small contact-list search in mobile apps, checking if user input is in a list of valid options, scanning small config files, reading files line by line.

Real-time data (sensor readings, log entries) arrives chronologically, not sorted -- backend services scan it linearly by necessity.

It's also the standard teaching algorithm for comparison flow, stop conditions, and the relationship between input size and runtime.

subsections.title: Mistake: Forgetting to stop after a match
subsections.content: Once you need the *first* match, return immediately -- continuing to scan wastes work and can return the wrong index.

subsections.title: Mistake: Returning the element instead of the index
subsections.content: A common slip: returning `arr[i]` instead of `i`. Check whether the task wants the index, the value, or a boolean.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring the not-found case
subsections.content: Always define what happens when nothing matches. `-1` is the standard sentinel, since real indices are never negative.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Linear Search checks elements **sequentially**, with zero preprocessing.
**Reverse Traversal** and **Boundary Clamping** handle specialized queries.
Simple and reliable, but **not ideal for repeated searches** on large data.
